text: A platoon comes home from Korea decorated, and every man in it praises Sergeant Raymond Shaw in the same words. Captain Bennett Marco, who led them, sleeps badly: what he sees at night does not match what he repeats by day, and the film is in no hurry to tell him which account to keep. Frankenheimer builds it out of public occasions and private nightmares, then lets the cutting carry the argument. Edits land a beat early. A room becomes another room mid-sentence, and the effect is less dreamlike than clerical, as though someone had filed the footage wrong on purpose. Two hours and six minutes, made in 1962, with the war it opens on not yet a decade cold. The jokes in it are real jokes. That is the part that unsettles.

An undertaker marries an executioner's daughter, and the post comes attached to her. He does not want it. That reluctance is the engine of the whole picture: Luis García Berlanga sets a mild, agreeable man inside a chain of small arrangements — steady work, a wife, a father-in-law who cannot retire until somebody takes the job — and closes each link behind him without ever raising its voice. Nothing is refused out loud. The comedy is procedural rather than savage, ninety-one minutes of family obligation conducted at the volume of an office, and it was made in Spain in 1963, in the country whose civil service the joke belongs to. It sits on Caimán's hundred best Spanish films. What it grasps is how a decent man can be walked toward a monstrous duty by relatives who only want to see him settled.

Letty Mason relocates to West Texas and finds that the country gets indoors: sand at the sills, a wind that does not stop at the door of her cousin's ranch. He is glad to have her. His wife is not, and Victor Sjöström lets that coldness harden over days rather than announcing it, while three men press attentions on Letty that she has no comfortable way to refuse. It is filed as a western and a romance; what it plays as is a siege. Silent, seventy-six minutes, 1928 — no dialogue to lean on, so weather and faces divide the work between them, and both are held past the point of ease. Cahiers du Cinéma keeps it among the hundred most beautiful films in the world, which reads oddly for something this abrasive until a room fills with dust and the light inside it starts doing the acting.

A tractor arrives in the village, and in 1930 that sentence is policy as much as plot. Oleksandr Dovzhenko made Earth in Ukrainian during the Soviet campaign to collectivize the land; his young protagonist belongs to the Communist youth, and his first use of the machine is to plow through the boundary markers of privately held fields — lines drawn by neighbors, in soil everyone there knows by hand. Seventy-nine minutes is short for a story about a village changing owners, and Dovzhenko does not spend the time on argument. He spends it on faces, on crops, on the intervals between events, until the errand the film was built to run keeps falling behind the ground it was shot on. It sits on the hundred best films in the history of Ukrainian cinema. The tractor is a machine and also an announcement.

Eight years of marriage, and the drive south is the first long stretch Katherine and Alex Joyce have spent alone with each other. They are English; the errand is practical and Italian — a villa outside Naples, inherited from his uncle, to be sold — and it strands them in a house with almost nothing to do. Rossellini gives it eighty-five minutes and next to no incident. Days get filled with outings and meals; the marriage is examined through logistics rather than confession, and most of the talk is the small business of who is going where, and when. The pressure is the pressure of a foreigner with no work: every hour not spent on the sale is an hour two people have to be in the same room. What surfaces is not a secret. It is that neither of them has ever had to look.

A boarding school runs on rules fine enough to be broken one at a time, and four boys pick the day of the official celebration to break them all at once. Jean Vigo made it in France in 1933 and gave it forty-eight minutes, long enough for a grievance and a plan and nothing else. The adults are seen from child height: small, self-important, absurd in the specific way authority looks to people with no power at all. Nothing about the boys is softened into charm, either. Their revolt has the logic of children — total in commitment, arbitrary in its targets, with no thought spent on Monday. At that length there is no room for a moral, and Vigo shows no sign of wanting one. It plays less like a report on school than like something remembered at speed.

Nobody in the town has gone missing, and that is exactly the difficulty. Everyone is present, at the same work, in the same houses, and the people who say something is wrong cannot point to a single absence. Don Siegel runs eighty flat minutes on that problem, with a small-town doctor at the center and a threat that has no appearance of its own — which pushes the horror onto performance, onto the faint wrongness of a familiar person behaving correctly. For a while it proceeds like a case: complaints, examinations, a physician trying to square testimony against what he can verify. Then it stops being a case and becomes a matter of speed. It is 1956, science fiction on a short leash, and the film never says what the duplication is finally for. It does not have to.

The trophies are the visible prize and the smallest thing at stake in the room. Jennie Livingston spent seven years inside Harlem's African American and Latinx drag-ball scene, and what accumulates over seventy-eight minutes is less a record of contests than of an economy: houses with mothers, categories with rules, reputations that have to be defended in public because there is nowhere private to keep them. Willi Ninja, Pepper LaBeija, Dorian Corey and Venus Xtravaganza address the camera as people who settled their positions long before anyone turned up with equipment. Around them, at the close of the 1980s, sit poverty, AIDS, homophobia, transphobia and racism, none of which the film pauses to introduce. Nobody here is explaining themselves to an outsider. They are explaining the rules to each other, and the camera was let in.

A family fortune can decay for a generation before anybody living on it agrees to notice. The Amberson heir, young and thoroughly indulged, puts his energy into a private project: keeping his widowed mother apart from the man she has always loved, an interference he conducts as if it were a duty owed to the family name. Orson Welles takes eighty-eight minutes over it — less time than that slow arithmetic wants, a town outgrowing the people who used to own it, a house that has to be crossed to reach anyone in it. Doorways, staircases, conversations that continue out of earshot. Manners are the weapon of choice, and nothing is raised above a civil tone. The film is coldest not about the boy's cruelty but about the courtesy of the adults around him, who keep treating it as a phase.

Two hired men are sent to Bruges to wait, and nobody tells them how long. Ken takes to the place — old, well kept, quiet in the way tourists pay for — and Ray is climbing the walls before the first afternoon is out. Most of the film is that mismatch: sightseeing as punishment, two colleagues filling days with argument because the alternative is thinking about the job just behind them. Martin McDonagh writes for the stage as well, and it shows in the timing; the comedy sits in who speaks after the pause, and the cruelty in how funny a man can be while coming apart. A hundred and eight minutes, most of them spent on people who are, technically, off duty. The order they are waiting for is coming. The film is in no rush to hand it over.

The river is scheduled to disappear under a lake, and that deadline is the only reason men from town are on it in canoes. Lewis Medlock wants to see the Cahulawassee before the water rises; the friends he brings come along as a favor, fit enough for a weekend and equipped for nothing past it. John Boorman films the trip as labor — how a canoe behaves in current, how far a shout carries, how long it takes to climb anything at all — so the country never settles into scenery. It is 1972, and these are men who have carried office confidence into a valley whose residents have already watched it be sold. The subject is competence, and the speed with which the question of who has any gets asked again. Nothing about the water is symbolic. That is what makes it hard going.

A man still makes his living shining shoes at a French port, and the film treats that as an ordinary way to be alive in 2011. His wife is ill. A boy from Africa is somewhere around the docks with the police looking for him, and the shoeshiner's answer to this is not anguish but logistics: money, a place to keep him, which neighbors can be asked for what. Aki Kaurismäki works in French with Finnish production behind him, in flat frontal frames and colors that belong to no particular decade, and keeps his cast pitched level, which holds sentiment at arm's length while the story walks straight into kindness. Ninety-four minutes, no speeches, few explanations. A whole small neighborhood gets quietly enlisted, and not one person in it makes a virtue of having helped.
